oneLine.text: Treat engineering management as a system of constraints you can diagnose and redesign.

sections.body: Engineering organizations behave like systems: team size, staffing, technical debt and process interact in predictable ways. Leaders get durable results by diagnosing the state a team is in and changing the structure around it, through sizing, migrations, metrics and process, rather than relying on individual heroics.

ideas.title: Size teams deliberately
ideas.summary: Larson recommends managers support roughly six to eight engineers and warns against very small teams, which struggle with on-call load and absences.
ideas.caveat: The numbers come from fast-growing technology companies and may not fit smaller or very different organizations.

ideas.title: Four states of a team
ideas.summary: A team is falling behind, treading water, repaying debt or innovating, and each state has a different fix: hire, reduce work in progress, add time, or add slack.
ideas.caveat: Real teams can sit between states, and diagnosing the state is a judgment call.
ideas.example: A team falling behind is unlikely to be rescued by process changes alone if it simply lacks people.

ideas.title: Think in systems
ideas.summary: Modelling problems as stocks and flows, such as a hiring pipeline, helps leaders predict the effect of a change before making it.
ideas.caveat: Models simplify; they guide judgment rather than replace it.

ideas.title: Migrations are how debt gets paid
ideas.summary: Large technical migrations are the main scalable way to retire technical debt, and they succeed when they are de-risked early, made easy with tooling, and driven to completion.
ideas.caveat: A migration left half-finished leaves two systems to maintain instead of one.

ideas.title: Set baselines before goals
ideas.summary: Measure where things stand before committing to targets, so goals are grounded and progress is visible.
ideas.caveat: Metrics invite gaming when they become the goal themselves.
